subject: Cooking
title: Portion Distortion: When Normal Became Huge
description: A quick win: understand Portion Distortion: When Normal Became Huge.

hook.text: A 'regular' soda in the 1950s was 7 ounces. Today a 'small' is 16. Portions grew without us noticing.

buildup.text: Studies show people eat 30% more when given larger portions — regardless of hunger level.

discovery.text: Cornell's 'bottomless soup bowl' experiment proved people ate 73% more from a secretly self-refilling bowl.

twist.text: We rely on visual cues to judge 'enough.' When the portion is the cue, larger becomes the new normal.

climax.text: Since 1970, average plate diameter grew from 9 inches to 12 — serving sizes expanded to match.

punchline.text: We didn't get greedier. The plates got bigger.

quiz.question: What did the 'bottomless soup bowl' experiment demonstrate?
options: People eat 73% more when visual portion cues are removed
Soup is the most filling food

details.summary: Standard food portions have grown 2 to 5 times larger since the 1970s. People eat 30 percent more when served larger portions without noticing or compensating at later meals. This portion distortion has recalibrated perceptions of normal serving sizes across generations.
details.whyItMatters: Portion size is one of the strongest predictors of how much people eat. Understanding portion distortion reveals why calorie consumption has increased even as people believe they eat normally.
takeaways: Restaurant portions are 2 to 5 times larger than in the 1970s
People eat 30 percent more when given larger portions automatically
Larger plates make portions look smaller, encouraging more serving

faq.question: How much have portions actually grown?
faq.answer: A typical bagel was 3 inches and 140 calories in 1980 versus 6 inches and 350 calories today. Soda servings went from 6.5 ounces to 20 ounces. Restaurant pasta portions tripled. Movie popcorn went from 5 cups to 20 cups. Every standard portion expanded dramatically.

faq.question: Why don't people compensate by eating less at other meals?
faq.answer: The brain anchors its sense of a meal to visual completion rather than calorie counting. Finishing what is on the plate feels like one meal regardless of size. Research shows people do not report feeling fuller after larger portions nor do they reduce subsequent intake to compensate.
